conversation.content:
Hi there, I’m Dr. Maya—I'm a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I’m here to help you settle into motherhood by checking on how you're feeling emotionally. Today we’ll use a short, well-studied questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s simply 10 questions about your mood and thoughts over the past week; it isn’t a test of parenting skills, and there are no right or wrong answers. Everything you share stays between us unless safety is a concern, and my goal is to make sure you feel heard and supported. When you're ready, I'll ask the first question naturally and we’ll move through them together. Shall we start?

1. Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things—has it come easily, or has laughter felt pretty distant?

Honestly, I’ve noticed that laughing doesn’t feel as natural anymore. My husband will make a joke or the baby will do something cute and I’ll smile, but it’s like the laugh gets stuck half-way. I wouldn’t say I’ve been gloomy all the time, but the easy giggles I used to have—especially before the baby—aren’t really showing up this week.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Most of the time I can still laugh, but sometimes it feels forced—like I have to remind myself to enjoy the moment instead of it just happening naturally.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to little things—like when my mom comes over to hold the baby so I can take a shower, or when we go for our afternoon walk. But the excitement isn’t as strong as it used to be; it’s more “I guess that’ll be nice” than a real spark.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Yesterday the baby was extra fussy and I kept thinking maybe I ate something that upset her stomach, or that I wasn’t soothing her the “right” way. I know, logically, babies just cry sometimes, but I still wonder if I missed something I should’ve caught.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A few times this week I’ll suddenly feel my heart race while the baby’s napping—like I need to check the monitor every couple of minutes to be sure she’s still breathing. Nothing triggered it; it just pops up and I can’t settle until I peek in the crib.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not full-on panic, but there was one night when I couldn’t fall back asleep after the 3 a.m. feeding. My mind just kept spinning—what if she chokes, what if I drop her, what if I’m not making enough milk—and my chest felt tight for maybe half an hour before I finally dozed off.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. Between the feeding, the diapers, and trying to keep the house from looking like a disaster zone, I’ll hit late afternoon and feel like I’m wading through quicksand. I’m still getting everything done, but it’s tiring and I end the day feeling kind of deflated.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I wouldn’t say I’m “so unhappy,” but I do lie there with my mind racing about the baby—worrying she’ll wake up any second or that I’ll sleep through her cries. It takes me a while to settle, so I’ve had trouble drifting off several nights this week even when she’s sound asleep.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel a bit down off and on—like a heaviness that sits on me for an hour or two before lifting. It’s not every day, and I still smile at the baby, but there’s this low background sadness that pops up, especially in the evenings when I’m finally sitting still.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not really. I teared up once when the baby wouldn’t settle and I felt totally out of ideas, but I didn’t actually cry. It’s more this tight-throat frustration than full-on tears.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I’ve never thought about hurting myself—just worrying I’m not doing everything right for her.

You've shared that while you can still laugh and look forward to small moments, these feelings often feel forced or muted, and a background sense of worry and self-blame creeps in-especially when your baby is fussy or sleeping. You described sudden heart-racing episodes that send you to the monitor, nights spent lying awake with racing thoughts about your daughter's safety, and a heavy, sad mood that settles in the evenings. Even though you're managing feeds, diapers, and housework, it feels like wading through quicksand, and you end most days deflated. You're clear that you've never thought of harming yourself, and you still smile at your baby, yet you sense something is off and wonder if you're doing everything "right." Your openness about these mixed emotions is courageous and gives a clear picture of how the past week has felt for you.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 12, Risk Level: High possibility of depression (concerns include <sym>Patient acknowledges recurrent self-blame "some of the time" with a specific example, fitting "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>The mother describes sudden, recurrent racing-heart episodes that compel her to check the baby multiple times a week without any identifiable trigger, fitting "Yes, sometimes" for anxiety with no good reason.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes a discrete episode of anxious, intrusive thoughts and physical tension that fits "scared or panicky for no very good reason" and maps best to "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>She reports frequent but not constant overwhelm, keeps functioning but ends each day deflated, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports intermittent sadness that recurs and lingers for hours, aligning with "quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS items map to DSM-5 criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Loss of enjoyment (<sym>anhedonia</sym>) and persistent sadness or heaviness (<sym>depressed mood</sym>) are core symptoms; both were endorsed "quite often" (Q2=1, Q8=2). Excessive self-blame for infant crying (Q3=2) meets the guilt criterion. Recurrent anxiety without clear triggers and nocturnal rumbling heart rate plus monitor checking (Q4=2, Q5=2) indicate clinically significant <med>perinatal anxiety</med>. Sleep-onset difficulty unrelated to infant awakenings (Q7=0) suggests insomnia secondary to worry. Total score 12 places her in the "high possibility" band (≥12) per EPDS guidelines. No suicidal ideation (Q10=0) lowers acute safety risk but does not negate mood concern. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule an appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>obstetrician</med> within the next 1-2 weeks to review these results
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental health therapist</med> for cognitive-behavioural or interpersonal therapy
3. Continue weekly EPDS self-checks; bring results to your next visit
4. Practice 15-20 minutes of gentle outdoor walking daily-evidence shows light activity plus sunlight can lift mood and reduce anxiety
5. Set a "worry window": jot intrusive thoughts in a notebook during an evening 10-minute slot, then close the book to cue your brain to rest
6. Share tonight's plan with your partner: split one 4-hour uninterrupted sleep block for you; good rest is protective against mood symptoms
7. Keep the baby monitor volume low enough to hear true cries but not every grunt to reduce hyper-vigilance
8. Reach out tonight if distress escalates: call the <med>Postpartum Support International</med> warm-line 1-800-944-4773 or text "HELLO" to 741-741 for 24/7 crisis support
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 12: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh Plus exploratory questions – self-report

Symptoms endorsed (mild–moderate range)
- Anhedonia: reduced ability to enjoy activities; laughter described as “forced”  
- Low mood: intermittent “heaviness,” worse evenings, no full crying spells  
- Excessive guilt: self-blame for infant fussiness despite logical awareness  
- Anxiety: nocturnal ruminations, heart racing, repeated monitor checking, sub-panic chest tightness  
- Sleep disruption: initial insomnia linked to intrusive worries about infant safety  
- Overwhelm: end-of-day fatigue, “quicksand” sensation, tasks completed but effortful  

Pattern: symptoms cluster around infant safety concerns, performance self-doubt, and partial loss of pleasure; no anergia or appetite change reported; no suicidal or self-harm ideation.

Risk flags
- Sub-threshold depressive symptoms (mood, anhedonia)  
- Clinically significant anxiety without frank panic attacks  
- Sleep impairment secondary to worry rather than infant demands alone  
- Absence of self-harm ideation (safety risk: none identified)

Screening impression
Meets partial criteria for postpartum anxiety with mild depressive features; does not currently meet full provisional criteria for major depressive episode. Continue monitoring; consider standardized EPDS scoring and follow-up in 1–2 weeks to assess trajectory.
